stem: Cholera bacteria release the toxin, choleragen, when they are in the intestine.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Name the bacterium that is the pathogen of cholera.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Describe the way in which cholera is transmitted from an infected person to an uninfected person.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem:
Gangliosides are glycolipids that bind choleragen. These glycolipids are found on many cell surface membranes.

When choleragen is released from the bacteria in the intestine, it binds to gangliosides on epithelial cells and enters these cells as shown in Fig. 6.1.

{{figure:figure_6_1.png}}

Fig. 6.1

not drawn to scale
parts.text: Suggest how choleragen interacts with gangliosides on intestinal epithelial cells.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Name the process by which choleragen enters the intestinal epithelial cell as shown in Fig. 6.1.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Once inside the cells choleragen is activated. One effect is to increase the movement of chloride ions through channel proteins out of cells.
parts.text: Suggest **and** explain the likely consequences on the intestinal epithelial cells of the loss of chloride ions through the channel proteins.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Health authorities recommend that antibiotics, such as tetracycline, are **only** to be used for treating people with severe cases of cholera.
parts.text: Explain why it is recommended that antibiotics should **not** be given to people with mild cases of cholera or to protect people from cholera.
